reason: Glands described as cup-like or cyathiform; the gland shape is cup-shaped.
Lobes can be erect, spreading or reflexed; position is meaningful for lobes.
Lobe orientation (ascending, spreading, divaricate) is correctly annotated.
Achene surfaces are punctate or puncticulate (dotted).
Imbricate (overlapping) bracts describe how the bracts are arranged; this is a spatial pattern.
Lobes and apices can be spreading. I judged this from the examples, because the part label is empty.
Rudimentary or vestigial stamens, for example in pistillate flowers, are standard.
Texture such as membranous or papillose is meaningful for corona, margin and appendage parts. The part label is empty, so I judged this from the examples.
Fleshy segments are normal. The part class is generic, so the examples carry the judgement.
'Bristlelike' means the stipule is shaped like a bristle, which is not the same as bearing bristles. A rule would need to separate '-like' shape comparisons from 'with bristles'.
Spore surfaces can be rugose or rugate (wrinkled).
Sporophylls are described as monomorphic, homomorphic or dimorphic; morphology covers this.
A hyaline or transparent leaf apex or hair-point is a normal description.
The examples describe the spur of a petal (bearded) or general pubescence, not a short shoot. This looks like a wrong mapping of 'spur' to short shoot.
Seed scales (megasporophylls) in cones are described by shape, such as reniform or flabellate.
Surface hairiness (hispidulous) on the adaxial leaf surface is correct.
Subglabrous and glabrous are hairiness (pilosity) values for this surface or organ.
Margins are described as subentire, which is a margin form close to entire.
Pinnules and similar parts can be lanceolate.
Spathes and similar organs can be reflexed.
A labellum can be elliptic.
Bract apices are acuminate.
Glands are described as large; the size is that of the gland.
Veins and veinlets can be dense (closely spaced).
Stelidia (orchid column projections) are triangular or deltoid.
Utricles can be pubescent.
A calyx rim can be subentire, meaning almost without teeth.
A rostellum can be erect.
Corona lobes have 2-D shapes such as ovate.
Nectaries bear fimbriate projections; this is acceptable, though the quality is on the projections.
Follicle colour is meaningful.
A costa can project or protrude on one side.
The examples often describe enlarged cells in the cortex, not the cortex itself. A rule would need to tell cell size from organ size.
There is one flora and one French example ('foliacé'), and the part is unclear. It needs more examples to confirm that 'leaf-like' fits.
A lamina can be large.
The examples are colours or tones (pale, dark, bright red) and belong under colour. The generic optical-quality term is too vague; a rule would map colour words to colour.
Leaf blades can be cleft.
A tube can be cylindrical.
Bases can be woody (ligneous).
Fruits and capsules can be deciduous.
An ovary can be hispidulous.
Bracts, midribs and bracteoles can be dark.
Lobes can be flabellate (fan-shaped).
A perigynium can be pubescent.
Ligule height or length in mm is meaningful.
Spikes can be globose.
Anthers can be ciliate.
A corolla can be cream-coloured.
The examples report druses or a 'superficial cortex' in the cortex, not the presence of the cortex as a trait. Presence of a cortex is not a useful quality here, so this reading is wrong.
Spikelets are bisexual or perfect.
Sepals can bear bristles. Some 'bristlelike' examples are shape comparisons, but most are correct.
Pseudobulbs are present or absent.
A viscidium can be ovate or elliptic.
Lobes can be falcate.
Secondary veins diverge or spread from the midvein.
Nuts can be subglobose or spheroid.
Stipules can be asymmetrical.
Achene bodies can be curved.
A spadix has a shape such as straight, curved or conic.
A leaf apex can be bilobed.
